title: Is it better to be feared than loved?
teaches: The Prince, read in its setting

blocks.text: In February 1513, in Florence, a former government official called Niccolò Machiavelli was arrested. His name had been found on a list kept by two young men plotting against the Medici family, who had just retaken the city. He was tortured with the *strappado*: his wrists were tied behind his back and he was hoisted up by them and dropped, six times. He confessed nothing, and probably knew nothing. A few weeks later a Medici was elected pope, and in the celebrations Machiavelli was freed in a general amnesty.[^strappado]

blocks.caption: Machiavelli as Santi di Tito painted him in the later 16th century, decades after his death.

blocks.text: He retired, ruined, to his small farm outside the city. On 10 December 1513 he described his days there in a letter to a friend. In the mornings he went to his wood and argued with the woodcutters. In the afternoons he went to the inn and played cards and backgammon with the butcher, the miller and two brickmakers, quarrelling loudly over pennies. "When evening comes, I return home and go into my study. On the threshold I strip off my muddy, sweaty, everyday clothes, and put on the robes of court and palace", and then he entered, he wrote, the courts of the ancients, asked them the reasons for their actions, and they answered him. From these conversations he had written "a little work", *On Principalities*. We know it as *The Prince*.

Machiavelli's Italy was a patchwork of city states, duchies, papal lands and kingdoms, at war with each other and, since 1494, invaded again and again by the armies of France and Spain. Cities changed hands in months. Florence itself had thrown out the Medici in 1494 and set up a republic, which Machiavelli had served for fourteen years as a senior official and diplomat, sent to the courts of the French king, the emperor and the pope. He had organised a citizen militia. In 1512 a Spanish army sacked the nearby town of Prato, the militia ran, and the republic fell.

*The Prince* is a handbook for a new ruler in such a world: someone who has just taken power, has no long-standing family claim to it, and must hold on. Machiavelli dedicated it to Lorenzo de' Medici, the young ruler of Florence, probably hoping for a job. Lorenzo is said to have paid it little attention. The book was not printed until 1532, five years after Machiavelli's death.

What shocked readers was chapter 15. Many writers, Machiavelli said, have imagined republics and principalities that never existed. He would write about how people actually live, not how they ought to. "A man who wishes to make a profession of goodness in everything must necessarily come to grief among so many who are not good. Therefore it is necessary for a prince, who wishes to maintain himself, to learn how not to be good, and to use this knowledge and not use it, according to the necessity of the case."

Chapter 17 asks the question in this lesson's title. It would be best, Machiavelli says, to be both loved and feared, but since the two rarely go together, if you must choose, it is much safer to be feared. People are ungrateful and fickle; they will offer you their blood and their children while danger is far off, and turn on you when it comes near. Love is held by a chain of obligation, which people break whenever it suits them; fear is held by a dread of punishment, which never fails. But a prince must avoid being hated, and that is easy: he need only keep his hands off his subjects' property and their women, since "men forget the death of their father more quickly than the loss of their inheritance".

blocks.caption: Chapter 17's question. Your answer is saved on the Verdicts page.

options.ask: A new leader takes over in a dangerous time and cannot be both. Is it better to be feared than loved?
choices: Feared: fear is more reliable than affection
Loved: people work harder and stay loyal for a leader they like
Neither: being respected and trusted matters more than either
Not sure
who: You chose Machiavelli's answer, with his warning never to be hated.
You chose the answer most modern management books give. Machiavelli would say affection holds only while times are good.
You chose an answer Machiavelli would partly accept: he thought a reputation for keeping order mattered more than either feeling.
Machiavelli thought it depended on the times, too.

blocks.text: His model was Cesare Borgia, the pope's son, who conquered the Romagna in the years around 1500. Finding it full of robbery and feuds, Borgia sent a cruel and efficient governor, Remirro de Orco, who restored order quickly. Then, to show that the cruelty had not been his own, Borgia had Remirro cut in two and left in the square at Cesena one morning, with a block of wood and a bloody knife beside him. "The ferocity of this spectacle left the people at once satisfied and stunned."

parts.title: What it says and what it doesn't

blocks.text: Few books are quoted so often by people who have not read them. The adjective "Machiavellian" came to mean cunning and unscrupulous within a century, and the Church put his works on its Index of Forbidden Books in 1559. Some of what is attributed to him is not in the book at all.

blocks.caption: Six claims often made about The Prince. Sort each by whether the book says it.

items.name: If you cannot be both loved and feared, it is safer to be feared
items.why: Chapter 17, with the condition that the prince must never be hated.

items.name: A prince must learn how not to be good, and when to use that knowledge
items.why: Chapter 15, the passage that shocked his readers.

items.name: A prince should be both a fox, to see traps, and a lion, to frighten wolves
The ends justify the means
items.why: The nearest is chapter 18's remark that, in judging rulers, people look to the outcome.

items.name: A ruler should make himself hated, so that no one dares oppose him
items.why: He says the opposite: being hated is the one thing a prince must avoid.

items.name: Monarchy is always the best form of government
items.why: His longer book, the Discourses on Livy, argues that a republic is best when it can be had.

blocks.text: That last point is the puzzle of Machiavelli. His other major book, the *Discourses on Livy*, written in the same years, is a long argument for republics, governed by citizens under laws, with the people's liberty protected by institutions. Readers have offered different ways to fit the two together. Some say *The Prince* was a job application, written for the Medici's eyes. Some, among them Rousseau, said it was a satire, exposing how princes really behave so that free people could see it. Many scholars now read the two books as one view: a republic is best, but in a crisis, such as a founding or a collapse, one person must act alone, and must be ready to do things that ordinary morality forbids.[^satire]

Machiavelli's deepest challenge is whether political leaders may, or must, do things that would be wrong for anyone else. In 1973 the American political philosopher Michael Walzer, borrowing the title of a play by Sartre, called this the problem of **dirty hands**. His example was a newly elected leader who has promised to end a colonial war, and whose officials capture a rebel who knows where bombs have been hidden in apartment buildings across the capital. Walzer asked whether the leader may order him tortured to find them, and answered that the leader may be right to do it and still be guilty, and should feel guilty: a politician who did such a thing easily would be the wrong person to trust with power.

blocks.caption: Walzer's problem. Your answer is saved on the Verdicts page.

options.ask: Can a leader be right to do something that is morally wrong, for the sake of the people they govern?
choices: Yes: sometimes they must, and should still feel the guilt
No: what is wrong for a private person is wrong for a ruler
Not sure
who: You chose Walzer's answer, and Machiavelli's, minus the guilt.
You chose Kant's view in lesson 15, and that of many of Machiavelli's Christian critics.
Walzer himself said the problem is real precisely because neither answer is comfortable.

blocks.text: Machiavelli is respected history and still argued over. He is read as the founder of political realism, the view that politics must be studied as it is, which runs through Hobbes in lesson 11 to the realist school in international relations today. The dirty-hands problem is an active debate in ethics, especially about torture, war and secret services. Many historians now read him as a republican who wrote one ruthless handbook for an emergency. Psychology took his name for a personality trait: since 1970 a standard questionnaire has measured "Machiavellianism", a tendency to manipulate others.[^mach]

blocks.caption: Four questions on Machiavelli
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What did Machiavelli say about being feared or loved in chapter 17 of The Prince?
choices: It is best to be both, but if you must choose it is safer to be feared, as long as you are not hated
A prince should always try to be hated, since hatred keeps people obedient
Love is more reliable than fear, because loyal subjects never betray their ruler
A prince should make himself feared by seizing his subjects' property
items.why: Fear holds by dread of punishment; love by obligation, which people break when it suits them.

items.ask: Which of these is NOT in The Prince?
choices: The ends justify the means
A prince must learn how not to be good
A prince should be both fox and lion
It is safer to be feared than loved, if you cannot be both
items.why: The nearest line is that people judge rulers by the outcome.

items.ask: How do many scholars now fit The Prince together with the Discourses on Livy?
choices: A republic is best, but in a crisis one person must act alone and may have to do what morality forbids
The Prince is Machiavelli's real view and the Discourses were written to please the Church
The two books were written by different authors
The Discourses is a satire of republics
items.why: The Discourses argues for republics; The Prince is a handbook for founding or saving a state.

items.ask: What is Walzer's problem of dirty hands?
choices: Whether a political leader can be right to do something morally wrong for the public good
Whether politicians should be paid for public service
Whether a leader should share power with a council
Whether war can ever be ended by treaty
items.why: Walzer said such a leader may be right, and still guilty.

summary: **Rulers must learn how not to be good.** They must use that knowledge as necessity demands, since The Prince is a handbook for a new ruler holding power in a divided, invaded Italy.
**It is safer to be feared than loved.** Machiavelli added that a ruler who cannot be both must never be hated, and should keep his hands off his subjects' property.
**Machiavelli never wrote that ends justify means.** His Discourses on Livy argue for republics, and most scholars read The Prince as a handbook for emergencies.
**A leader may be right to do wrong.** Michael Walzer's answer to the problem of dirty hands is that such a leader is still guilty.

strappado.title: The six drops
strappado.text: Machiavelli mentioned the torture in a letter and in sonnets he wrote in prison to Giuliano de' Medici. The strappado often dislocated the shoulders. That he bore it without confessing became a point of pride for him.

satire.title: The satire reading
satire.text: In The Social Contract (1762), Rousseau wrote that Machiavelli, pretending to give lessons to kings, gave great ones to the people, and called The Prince the book of republicans. The American historian Garrett Mattingly argued the same in 1958. Few historians now accept it, since the book reads too seriously.

mach.title: The Mach scale
mach.text: The psychologists Richard Christie and Florence Geis built the Mach IV questionnaire in 1970, partly from statements adapted from The Prince, such as agreeing that the best way to handle people is to tell them what they want to hear.
